analogy.p: A **monoclonal antibody** is like a guided missile. The **antibody** is the guidance system that is programmed to recognise one particular target (the **antigen** on a cancer cell). The **drug or radioactive substance** attached to it is the warhead. Because the guidance system only locks onto its one target, the warhead is delivered to the cancer cells and not to the healthy cells around them. The analogy breaks down because a missile is a single object made once, whereas monoclonal antibodies are made as huge numbers of identical molecules from a clone of cells, and unlike a perfect missile they can still cause unwanted side effects.
analogy.t: A guided missile with a drug warhead

bullets: **Monoclonal antibodies** are produced from a **single clone of cells**, so every antibody molecule is identical.
They are **specific to one binding site on one protein antigen**, so they can target a **specific chemical or specific cells** in the body.

Production: **lymphocytes** are stimulated to make a particular antibody, combined with a **tumour cell** to make a **hybridoma cell**, which divides to produce **clones** that all make the same antibody; the antibody is then **collected and purified**.

Uses: **diagnosis** (for example pregnancy tests), **laboratories and research** (locating or identifying specific molecules in a cell or tissue by binding a fluorescent dye) and **treatment** (for example of cancer).
Evaluation point: monoclonal antibodies have caused **more side effects than expected**, so they are **not as widely used** as scientists first hoped.
Links to: the **immune system** (antibodies and antigens), **cancer** (uncontrolled cell division), **vaccination**, and **health and ethics** in science.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to know what a **monoclonal antibody** is, how it is **produced**, and how it is **used** in diagnosis, in laboratories and in treatment. This is a **Biology only (triple science)** topic, so it is not examined in the combined science papers. You must be able to describe the production steps in the correct order and then **evaluate** the uses, which means weighing up benefits and drawbacks. You are not expected to recall the details of any specific test, but you must be able to explain how an antibody could be used in an unfamiliar context. It matters because it shows how knowledge of the immune system has been turned into medical technology.

bullets: An **antigen** is a molecule (usually a protein) that triggers an immune response and has a particular shape.
An **antibody** is a protein made by lymphocytes with a binding site complementary to **one** antigen.
Antibodies bind to antigens on pathogens, which helps other white blood cells to destroy them.
In a normal infection the body makes **many different antibodies** (from many different lymphocytes) against the pathogen.
Monoclonal antibodies are different because they come from **one clone** of cells, so they are **all identical**.
Cancer cells have **antigens on their surface (tumour markers)** that are not found on normal body cells, which makes them a target.
Link to other topics: this builds directly on the topic of the **human defence system** and vaccination.
core.p: Every pathogen has molecules on its surface called **antigens**. When a pathogen enters the body, white blood cells called **lymphocytes** respond by making **antibodies**. An antibody has a **binding site** with a shape that is **complementary** to one particular antigen, rather like a key fitting one lock. Because the shapes must match, an antibody made against one pathogen will not normally bind to a different pathogen. Monoclonal antibodies take this natural idea and make **large amounts of one single, pure antibody** on purpose.

bullets: **Mono** = one; **clonal** = produced from a clone of identical cells.
Every monoclonal antibody molecule from the same clone has the **same shape of binding site**.
Specific means it fits only **one** antigen, so it ignores all other molecules in the body.
The target can be a **specific chemical** (such as a hormone) or **specific cells** (such as cancer cells).
The antibodies are made in a laboratory in large quantities, unlike a natural immune response which makes a mixture.
Exam wording: 'produced from a single clone of cells' and 'specific to one binding site on one protein antigen'.
core.p: The word **monoclonal** breaks into 'mono' (one) and 'clonal' (from a clone). A **clone** is a group of cells that are genetically identical because they all came from a single parent cell by cell division. All the cells in the clone therefore make exactly the same antibody, which is why the antibodies are described as monoclonal. The antibody has a binding site that fits **one specific binding site on one protein antigen**. This high specificity is the reason monoclonal antibodies can be used to find, mark or attack just one target among thousands of different molecules.

bullets: The chosen antigen is injected into a mouse (the animal is used as a living 'factory' for the right lymphocytes).
The mouse's lymphocytes are **stimulated to produce the antibody** against that antigen.
The lymphocytes that make the wanted antibody are collected, usually from the spleen.
Problem: these lymphocytes have a **limited ability to divide** in a culture, so they would soon stop producing antibody.
The next step solves this by joining them to cells that can divide **very rapidly**.
Ethical link: using animals raises ethical issues, which is one point to mention in an evaluation.
core.h: Step 1: getting lymphocytes that make the antibody you want
core.p: The first step is to obtain **lymphocytes that make the particular antibody** needed. To do this, an animal such as a **mouse** is injected with the **antigen** that the antibody must recognise. The mouse's immune system responds, and its lymphocytes start making antibodies specific to that antigen. Lymphocytes are then collected from the mouse. On their own, these lymphocytes make the right antibody but they **do not divide many times** in the laboratory, so they cannot be used to make large amounts of antibody.

bullets: **Lymphocyte** + **tumour cell** → **hybridoma cell**.
The lymphocyte provides the ability to make **one particular antibody**.
The tumour cell provides the ability to **divide rapidly and repeatedly**.
The hybridoma therefore does both jobs: makes antibody and keeps dividing.
Not every cell fuses successfully, so only the fused cells are kept for the next step.
Always say that the hybridoma is made from **two different types of cell**, not just 'a mixed cell'.
core.p: To solve the problem of lymphocytes not dividing, they are **combined (fused) with a tumour cell**. Tumour cells **divide rapidly and continually**, but they do not make the antibody that is wanted. The new cell formed by fusing the two is called a **hybridoma cell**. A hybridoma has **both** useful properties: it **makes the specific antibody** (from the lymphocyte) and it **divides rapidly** (from the tumour cell). This clever combination is the key idea of the whole process and is the most commonly examined step.

bullets: The **hybridoma cell divides to produce clones**, all of which make the same antibody (this is the mark scheme wording).
Cells making the correct antibody are identified and kept; the others are discarded.
Because the clone is **genetically identical**, the antibody it makes is identical every time.
The clones can be cultured in a nutrient medium in large vessels (fermenters) to give a large supply.
The cells keep dividing, so the supply of antibody is effectively **unlimited** as long as they are fed.
Link to other topics: growing cells in culture needs the sterile technique and nutrients you met in **culturing microorganisms**.
core.h: Step 3: selecting and cloning the hybridoma cells
core.p: The mixture of cells contains many different hybridomas, and only some of them make the **correct antibody**. The hybridoma cells are therefore tested, and those that produce the right antibody are kept and grown. Each selected hybridoma then **divides to produce clones**, and all of these clones produce the **same antibody**. This is where the word monoclonal comes from, because all the antibody comes from one clone of cells. The clones can be grown in large numbers because the tumour cell part of the hybridoma lets them divide again and again.

bullets: The antibody is **collected** from the culture medium.
It is then **purified** so that only the wanted antibody remains.
Large scale production is possible because the hybridoma cells can keep dividing.
The finished product is a supply of **identical antibodies** specific to one antigen.
Summary order to learn: **antigen injected → lymphocytes collected → fused with tumour cells → hybridoma cells → clones → antibody collected and purified**.
Exam tip: use the key words 'lymphocytes', 'tumour cell', 'hybridoma' and 'clone' in your answer.
core.h: Step 4: collecting and purifying the antibody
core.p: As the hybridoma cells grow, they **release the antibody into the culture medium** around them. The medium is collected, and the **monoclonal antibodies are separated and purified** from the other substances present. The result is a large quantity of **identical antibodies, all specific to the same antigen**. These can then be used in tests, in research or in medicines. This final step is easy to forget, but it is one of the four marking points in a typical 'describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced' question.

bullets: Lymphocyte alone: **correct antibody, but cannot divide enough** to give a large supply.
Tumour cell alone: **divides rapidly, but does not make the correct antibody**.
Hybridoma: **correct antibody AND rapid division**, so a large, continuous supply of one antibody.
This is why the first step is to stimulate lymphocytes with the antigen, and the second is to fuse them with tumour cells.
Fusion gives clones, and cloning guarantees that every antibody is identical (monoclonal).
Model sentence: 'The tumour cell allows the hybridoma to divide rapidly, and the lymphocyte allows it to make the specific antibody.'
core.h: Why use a hybridoma? The logic of the method
core.p: The whole method is built around the fact that **neither parent cell is enough on its own**. A lymphocyte can make the right antibody but cannot be grown in large numbers. A tumour cell grows rapidly but makes nothing useful. Joining them gives a single cell with the strengths of both. Explaining this reasoning is how you earn the 'explain why' marks, which are different from the 'describe' marks for simply listing the steps.

bullets: The antibodies are **specific to hCG**, so they do not bind to other hormones in the urine.
On the test strip, antibodies attached to coloured beads (mobile antibodies) bind to hCG if it is present.
This complex is then captured by fixed antibodies at the test line, so a **coloured line appears** (a positive result).
A control line shows that the test has worked, whether or not hCG is present.
Other diagnostic uses include detecting **hormones or pathogens** by binding to their specific antigens.
Advantage: tests are **quick, accurate, and can be used at home** or in a clinic.
Link to other topics: hCG is a hormone, so this links to the **endocrine system**.
core.h: Use 1: diagnosis, for example pregnancy tests
core.p: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to **detect specific chemicals in the body**, which makes them very useful in **diagnosis**. A well-known example is the **pregnancy test**. During pregnancy the body releases the hormone **hCG** (human chorionic gonadotropin), which passes into the urine. A pregnancy test contains monoclonal antibodies that bind only to hCG, so if hCG is present the test gives a visible result such as a coloured line. You do not need to recall details of specific tests, but you need to understand the principle that a specific antibody can pick out one chemical from a mixture.

bullets: The antibody is **bound to a fluorescent dye** that can be seen under a microscope.
It sticks only to the **specific molecule (antigen)** being looked for.
The dye then shows the **position** of the molecule in the cell or tissue.
Used in research to understand which proteins are present in healthy and diseased cells.
Also used in laboratories to **identify** the presence of particular pathogens or molecules in a sample.
The key idea to state is that the antibody is **specific**, so it only labels the target.
core.p: Scientists use monoclonal antibodies in the laboratory to **locate or identify specific molecules in a cell or tissue**. A fluorescent dye is attached to the antibody, and the antibody is added to the sample. The antibody binds only to its specific molecule, so when the sample is viewed under a microscope the dye shows exactly where that molecule is. This technique allows researchers to find out where particular proteins are found in cells and how they are involved in disease. Because the antibody is so specific, it can pick out one molecule among thousands.

bullets: The antibody is made **specific to the tumour marker** found on the cancer cells.
It carries a **radioactive substance**, a **toxic drug**, or a **chemical that stops cells growing and dividing**.
After injection it **binds only to cancer cells**, delivering the treatment to them.
**Other cells in the body are not harmed**, because the antibody does not bind to them.
This is more targeted than ordinary **chemotherapy**, which affects all rapidly dividing cells and so damages some healthy cells too.
Because the drug is delivered straight to the cancer cells, less drug may be needed.
Link to other topics: cancer is **uncontrolled cell division**, so this links to the cell cycle and non-communicable disease.
core.p: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to **treat diseases such as cancer**. Cancer cells have **antigens on their surface (tumour markers)** that are not found on normal body cells. A monoclonal antibody can be made that is specific to the tumour marker. The antibody is then **bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug, or a chemical that stops cells growing and dividing**. When injected into the patient, the antibody travels around the body but binds **only to the cancer cells**, so the treatment is delivered directly to the tumour. Normal cells that lack the tumour marker are not harmed.

bullets: Side effects have been **more common than scientists expected**.
As a result, monoclonal antibodies are **not used as widely as hoped**.
The production process is **complex and specialised**, which makes the antibodies expensive to produce.
The method uses **animals** (such as mice) to supply lymphocytes, which some people object to on ethical grounds.
They are still very valuable for **diagnosis and research**, where side effects are not a problem.
Treatments need testing in clinical trials before being widely used.
core.p: When monoclonal antibodies were first developed, scientists hoped they would be a '**magic bullet**' that could be used to treat many diseases without harming healthy cells. In practice, monoclonal antibodies have created **more side effects than expected**, so they are **not as widely used** as scientists had hoped. This is a good example of how scientific ideas have to be tested, and the real results can differ from predictions. The specification expects you to be able to state this and to weigh it against the benefits.

bullets: **Benefit:** highly specific, so they can target particular cells or chemicals.
**Benefit:** can deliver a drug straight to cancer cells, so healthy cells are less affected.
**Benefit:** diagnostic tests (like pregnancy tests) are quick and easy to use.
**Drawback:** more side effects than expected, so treatment use is limited.
**Drawback:** expensive and complex to make; animals are used in production.
**Conclusion:** state which is more important and why, for example 'they are very useful for diagnosis, but cancer treatment is limited by side effects'.
Use **comparative words**: 'more targeted than', 'less damage to', 'but', 'however'.
core.h: Evaluating the uses of monoclonal antibodies
core.p: Evaluation questions give you a use of monoclonal antibodies and ask you to judge it. A good answer gives **benefits**, **drawbacks** and a **justified conclusion**. Use the key idea of **specificity** for benefits, and the point about **side effects** for drawbacks. Link every point back to the context in the question (for example a cancer patient or a pregnancy test). A top mark answer also compares the new method with an older one, such as ordinary chemotherapy or a traditional test.

bullets: **Immune system:** antibodies are complementary in shape to antigens.
**Cell biology:** hybridoma cells divide by mitosis to give clones.
**Disease:** cancer cells have tumour markers; antibodies can find and attack them.
**Endocrine system:** hormones such as hCG can be detected using specific antibodies.
**Working scientifically:** evaluating risks, benefits and ethical issues of new technology.
**Applying knowledge:** for any new use, state the target antigen, what the antibody carries, and why it is specific.
Not required: names of specific cancer drugs or the exact method of selecting hybridomas.
core.h: Linking to other topics and extension
core.p: Monoclonal antibodies connect several parts of the course. The **immune system** provides the idea of antigens and antibodies, **cell division and the cell cycle** explain tumour cells and cloning, and **hormones** explain what pregnancy tests detect. Higher tier questions may ask you to **suggest** how a monoclonal antibody could be used in a situation you have not seen, so practise applying the same principles: choose an antigen, make a specific antibody, attach a label or drug, and explain why it only binds to its target.

exam: **Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced (4 marks):** (1) a specific antigen is used to stimulate lymphocytes to make the antibody; (2) the lymphocytes are combined with tumour cells; (3) this forms a hybridoma cell which divides to produce clones, all making the same antibody; (4) the antibody is collected and purified.
**Explain why a hybridoma cell is made (3 marks):** the lymphocyte makes the specific antibody; the tumour cell divides rapidly; so the hybridoma makes a lot of the antibody.
**Explain why a monoclonal antibody only binds to cancer cells (2 marks):** it is specific to one antigen (tumour marker) on the cancer cell, and normal cells do not have this antigen.

**Describe how monoclonal antibodies can treat cancer (3 marks):** antibody specific to a tumour marker; carries a radioactive substance, toxic drug or chemical that stops cell division; binds only to cancer cells so other cells are not harmed.
**Describe a use in laboratories (2 marks):** the antibody is bound to a fluorescent dye and added to a tissue; it binds to the specific molecule so its position can be seen.

**Pregnancy test questions (2 to 3 marks):** the antibodies are specific to the hormone hCG; if hCG is in the urine it binds to the antibodies and a coloured line appears; the control line shows the test has worked.

**Evaluate (6 marks):** give at least two benefits (specific, targeted treatment, quick diagnostic tests) and two drawbacks (more side effects than expected, not widely used, animals used, expensive), then write a justified conclusion.

**Command words:** 'Describe' = say the steps in order; 'Explain' = give reasons using 'because' or 'so'; 'Evaluate' = benefits, drawbacks and a conclusion; 'Suggest' = apply your knowledge to a new situation.
**Use key words:** 'lymphocyte', 'tumour cell', 'hybridoma', 'clone', 'specific', 'antigen'. A correct idea without the key word can lose the mark.
**Do not just say 'it targets cancer':** say it binds to the specific antigen/tumour marker on the cancer cell and delivers the drug/radioactive substance there.
**Triple only:** this topic is Biology only, so check your paper before spending time on it.

mistakes.r: They are made from hybridoma cells, formed by combining a lymphocyte with a tumour cell.
mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies are made from lymphocytes only.

mistakes.r: The lymphocyte makes the specific antibody; the tumour cell allows rapid division.
mistakes.w: The tumour cell makes the antibody.

mistakes.r: The antibody carries a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical that stops cells dividing, and delivers it to the cancer cells.
mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies kill cancer cells by themselves.

mistakes.r: They are specific to one antigen, so they bind only to cells that have that antigen.
mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies attack all cells in the body.

mistakes.r: Monoclonal means the antibodies come from a single clone of cells, so they are all identical.
The antigen is injected into the mouse; the mouse's lymphocytes then make the antibody.
mistakes.w: Antibodies are injected into mice to make the hybridoma.

mistakes.r: They have caused more side effects than expected, so they are not as widely used as hoped.
mistakes.w: They have no side effects because they only target cancer cells.

mistakes.r: The pregnancy test uses antibodies specific to the hormone hCG in urine.
mistakes.w: The pregnancy test detects the baby's DNA.

mistakes.r: The hybridoma divides to produce clones, so it can supply antibody continuously.
mistakes.w: Hybridoma cells are only used once.

summary: AQA (Biology only): you must describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced (lymphocytes combined with tumour cells to make hybridoma cells that divide to give clones making the same antibody), explain that they are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, and describe and evaluate their uses in diagnosis (for example pregnancy tests), laboratories and research, and treatment (for example cancer). It matters because 'describe how' and 'evaluate' questions on this topic are worth up to six marks.

terms.d: An antibody produced from a single clone of cells, specific to one binding site on one protein antigen.
A molecule, often a protein on the surface of a cell or pathogen, that triggers an immune response and has a particular shape.
A protein made by lymphocytes with a binding site complementary in shape to one specific antigen.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
A group of cells that are genetically identical because they came from a single parent cell.
A cell that divides rapidly and uncontrollably.
A cell made by combining a lymphocyte with a tumour cell; it makes a specific antibody and divides rapidly.
Binding to only one particular antigen (or binding site) and not to other molecules.
The part of an antibody with a shape complementary to its antigen.
An antigen found on the surface of cancer cells that is not found on normal body cells.
Identifying a disease or condition, for example by detecting a particular chemical in the body.
The hormone released during pregnancy that is detected by pregnancy tests using monoclonal antibodies.
A dye that glows under certain light, attached to an antibody to show where a molecule is in a cell or tissue.
A cell that a treatment is aimed at, for example a cancer cell.
An unwanted effect of a drug or treatment.
To separate a substance from other substances so that only the wanted substance remains.

worked.ans: Model answer: The antigen is used to stimulate lymphocytes to produce the specific antibody. The lymphocytes are combined with tumour cells to make hybridoma cells. The hybridoma cell divides to produce clones, all of which produce the same antibody. The antibody is then collected and purified.
worked.q: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: a mouse is injected with the antigen, so its lymphocytes are stimulated to make the specific antibody.
Mark 2: the lymphocytes are combined with tumour cells.
Mark 3: this makes hybridoma cells, which divide to produce clones that all make the same antibody.
Mark 4: the antibody is collected from the culture and purified.

worked.ans: The lymphocyte is needed to make the specific antibody. The tumour cell is needed because it divides rapidly. The hybridoma cell can therefore make the specific antibody in large quantities.
worked.q: A scientist makes a hybridoma cell by combining a lymphocyte with a tumour cell. Explain why each type of cell is needed. (3 marks)
steps: Lymphocyte: it makes the specific antibody.
Tumour cell: it can divide rapidly and repeatedly.
Together: the hybridoma both makes the antibody and keeps dividing, so large amounts can be made.

worked.ans: Model answer: Monoclonal antibodies can be made specific to a tumour marker found on cancer cells, so they bind only to cancer cells. They can carry a toxic drug, a radioactive substance or a chemical that stops cells dividing, so the treatment is delivered directly to the cancer, which means that healthy cells are less likely to be harmed than with chemotherapy. However, they have caused more side effects than expected, so they are not used as widely as scientists hoped, and they are expensive to produce, with animals used in the process. Overall, the targeted action is a major advantage, but because of side effects and cost, they are best used where other treatments are less suitable and when the benefit outweighs the risk.
worked.q: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer. Evaluate this use. (6 marks)
steps: Benefit: the antibody is specific to the tumour marker on cancer cells.
Benefit: it carries a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical that stops cell division, and delivers it to the cancer cells.
Benefit: other cells are not harmed, unlike ordinary chemotherapy.
Drawback: more side effects than expected, so they are not as widely used as hoped.
Drawback: complex production, expensive; animals are used.
